summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create a standard set of regulatory powers that Commonwealth agencies can use across different laws.
Agencies would gain monitoring and investigation powers, plus enforcement tools such as civil penalties, infringement notices, enforceable undertakings and injunctions.
The powers would be rolled out progressively, with new or amended laws needing to trigger the bill's provisions through primary legislation.
changes: Establishes a framework of standard regulatory powers for Commonwealth agencies.
Provides monitoring powers to check compliance with legislation and the accuracy of information given to the Commonwealth.
Provides investigation powers to gather evidence about suspected offences and civil penalty provisions.
Allows enforcement through civil penalties, infringement notices, enforceable undertakings and injunctions.
Requires new or amended laws to trigger the bill's provisions to activate the powers.
Allows agencies to choose not to trigger the bill's provisions if the powers are not appropriate or sufficient.
summary.affected: Commonwealth regulatory agencies and the regulatory schemes they administer.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Moved a bill to standardise Commonwealth regulatory monitoring, investigation and enforcement powers across the statute book, noting that inconsistent provisions can currently add up to 80 pages to individual pieces of legislation. Said the framework would be rolled out in three stages while preserving common law privileges against self-incrimination.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Said the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Bill 2014 revives a lapsed 2012 Labor initiative that could shorten a new Commonwealth act creating an agency by up to 80 pages, contrasting it with the government's largely symbolic March repeal day, and criticised the government for still pursuing abolition of the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Quoted the outgoing Independent National Security Legislation Monitor, Bret Walker QC, disputing the government's description of abolishing their office as cutting 'red tape', and said the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Bill 2014, almost identical to a 2012 Labor bill, was genuine reform that Labor supports.

speeches.speaker: Philip Ruddock
speeches.brief: Referred the Health Insurance Amendment (Extended Medicare Safety Net) Bill 2014 and the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Bill 2014 to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: Supported the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Bill 2014, noting it was originally developed under the previous Labor government following a 2006 report projecting regulation would grow to 55,000 pages, and said the reforms could reduce the size of a new Commonwealth act by up to 80 pages, while dismissing the government's red-tape repeal day as empty rhetoric.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Summed up debate on the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Bill 2014, saying it expressly preserves the privilege against self-incrimination and legal professional privilege, and confirmed the government will abolish the Office of the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor as part of streamlining Commonwealth agencies.
